tipBoundedBy: FROZEN 2026-04-30. Per-tick shards under docs/hygiene-history/ticks/YYYY/MM/DD/HHMMZ.md took over the write surface on 2026-04-29 and nothing has appended since; the file's own header now says so.
historyBoundedBy: The writer stopped. 87 versions on HEAD's history and no tick row appended since 2026-06-21; ticks/README.md's cadenced collator -- whose step 4 was literally 'Append to docs/hygiene-history/loop-tick-history.md' -- was removed in PR #17282, so the documented path back to rewriting it no longer exists.
liftsWhen: none -- there is no exit to wait for, because the row is already in its end state. It stays as a REGRESSION PIN: if this count ever moves, something started writing a frozen file again, and that is exactly the failure the ratchet exists to catch.
reason: The register's worked example of a BOUNDED row, and of what success looks like. Kept rather than deleted because containment was measured (2026-09-11) and refuted the assumption that motivated deleting it: 191 of its 212 rows have NO shard at all and ZERO rows have a shard at the same UTC minute, so 2026-04-21 .. 2026-04-27 exists only here. Its churn was the defect and its content is not -- which is why a row can be bounded, kept, and 648 KB at tip all at once without contradiction. CEILING NOTE, and it is the ratchet's own first worked example: this row was drafted at 86 and is pinned at 87 because PR #17282 wrote the FROZEN header into the file, which is a real write and moved the count. The check went red on the draft for exactly the right reason -- a file everyone had agreed was frozen got written -- and the honest resolution was to re-measure and re-pin with the cause named, not to widen the ceiling until it stopped complaining.

tipBoundedBy: One file per ecosystem, and the ecosystem set is a CLOSED TypeScript union (`Ecosystem` in src/Core.TypeScript/ace/outdated-inventory.ts). A new file can only appear by widening that union in a reviewed diff, so the working-tree size is capped by the type, not by a convention. 5 files today (cargo, go, npm, nuget, pypi); mise has no registry resolver and therefore no file.
rate: 0 versions/day observed -- this directory is CREATED by this commit, so one version exists and there is no history to average over. Saying otherwise would be an estimate wearing a measurement's clothes. What IS measured is the structural cap on the writer: the only thing that writes here is `ace outdated --refresh`, an explicit manual act with no cadence job, no hook and no workflow invoking it (checked: no reference in .github/workflows or githooks). For calibration, the nearest comparable row -- src/Core.TypeScript/ace/build-graph.json, also an ace-owned lock-shaped file -- measured 1.8 versions/day under an automated writer. Re-measure at 30 days; if this approaches that figure, something is refreshing it automatically and that is the finding.
costPerUnit: 4,528 bytes on disk for one full version across 5 blobs, measured with `git cat-file --batch-check='%(objectsize:disk)'` (cargo 213, go 237, npm 743, nuget 1029, pypi 2306). Raw sum is 32,571 bytes, i.e. the on-disk figure is 7.2x smaller; never quote the raw one. A refresh of ONE ecosystem costs only that ecosystem's blob -- the partition is what makes the per-event cost sub-linear in the dependency count. Pack-time delta compression against the prior version is NOT measured and will be smaller still.
breaksFirst: Nothing, at this rate. If an automated refresh were ever wired up, the first cost is review burden rather than bytes: a daily full-ecosystem refresh is ~1.6 MB/year on disk, which is negligible, but it produces a daily diff touching every dependency -- and a diff nobody reads is how a changed pin stops being noticed. The partition is the mitigation: refresh one ecosystem and only that file moves.
generator: PARTIAL, and the gap is the entire point of the file. `ace outdated --refresh` regenerates TODAY'S answer from the registries in ~90 seconds, so the CURRENT version is cheap to reproduce and costs nothing to keep. It cannot reproduce a PAST version: registries serve current state, and `what was npm's latest on 2026-06-09` is not a query any of these five APIs answers. So fidelity against the current row is 100% (subject to the network), and against any historical row it is zero. Upkeep: the command is run by a person, which is also its liveness risk -- a generator nobody runs is a check that did not run, which is exactly why the report prints the snapshot's age on every row and why --max-snapshot-age-days exists.
fidelityNeeded: APPROXIMATE, and deliberately so -- this is the opposite of the lockfile case. A lock must be exact because a build depends on it byte-for-byte; this snapshot only needs to be good enough to say 'you are roughly N behind', and it announces its own age so a reader can discount it. Nothing builds from it, nothing installs from it, and a wrong entry produces a wrong REPORT, never a wrong artifact. That is what makes the history genuinely disposable here: window it, and the only thing lost is the ability to ask when we first noticed a dependency drifting.
satelliteChain: db/ (hub: the tree's pinned versions, in the manifests themselves) -> registry/latest-known/<ecosystem>.json (satellite, depth 1: an external observation ABOUT those pins, changing at the registries' rate rather than ours) -> the rendered report (depth 2, never committed). Depth 1 is the right tier: this is a fast-changing attribute of a slow-changing key, which is the DV2.0 satellite definition, and it is split by ecosystem exactly as a satellite is split by change rate.
demotionPlan: Nothing to demote yet -- one version. If the history ever grows: the whole file is REPLACEABLE at depth 1 (a refresh reconstructs the current answer), so the demotion is simply to stop keeping old versions. The concrete move, when it is needed, is one file per refresh EVENT under registry/latest-known/<YYYY-MM>/<ecosystem>.json with the month folder pruned on a retention window -- the 'one per event in dated folders' shape this register prefers -- with the current answer symlinked or re-derived. Not done now because one version does not justify the indirection.
liftsWhen: When every ecosystem in the `Ecosystem` union has a resolver AND the file count stops changing, the tip bound stops being interesting; the history bound lifts only if this moves to dated event folders with a retention window, at which point this row is replaced rather than raised.
reason: A committed, offline-readable snapshot of each registry's latest known version, so `ace outdated` can answer 'which dependencies are behind' from a `git clone` at a tag with no package manager present -- the clone-at-tag-stays-sufficient requirement. It is rewritten whenever somebody runs an explicit refresh, which is the single-file-rewrite shape this register exists to make visible, so it is declared here rather than discovered later.

rate: 3 rows on the seed day 2026-09-11, which is the ONLY day measured -- the ledger is new, so this is a seed figure and not a trend. Stated that way on purpose: a rate quoted from one day is a starting point somebody must re-measure, and the ceiling below is set so the first crossing forces exactly that. The shape of the demand is one row per hypothesis-actually-disproven, which is bounded by agent-hours rather than by clock time.
costPerUnit: 561 bytes on disk per row (measured 2026-09-11 over the three seed blobs: 533 + 564 + 586 = 1683 bytes on disk, raw sum 2780 -- quote the on-disk one, never the raw). Rows are append-only and never rewritten, so a row costs its own blob ONCE and nothing else; the per-day directory adds three tree objects on the first row of a new year/month/day. Measured with git cat-file --batch-check='%(objectsize:disk)' over the blobs, as this file's own --cost flag does.
breaksFirst: Not clone size, at any plausible rate -- at 561 bytes a row, 10,000 refutations is 5.6 MB. What breaks first is the CONSUMER: renderBriefing is meant to be read at an agent's wake, and an unfiltered briefing crosses a useful context budget somewhere around a few hundred rows. That is why the demotion plan below is about what gets RENDERED rather than about what gets stored, and it is the honest answer to 'what fails first' for a directory no disk will ever notice.
generator: none -- and this is a real STEP 3 rather than a generator nobody looked for. The thing a row records is a hypothesis that was TRIED AND DROPPED, and a dropped approach leaves no artifact by construction: there is no diff, no test, no commit. Where a refutation did cause a code change the diff is a partial generator, but those are the CHEAP rows to rediscover; the expensive ones -- an approach abandoned after an hour with nothing committed -- are exactly the ones no generator can reproduce. Fidelity of any re-derivation against the abandoned-approach case is zero, so the bytes ARE the information.
fidelityNeeded: EXACT on the hypothesis and the refuting mechanism, because the row's entire job is to be RECOGNISED when the same idea is proposed again; a paraphrase that no longer matches the proposal fails silently, which is the worst failure available to a ledger of negative results. Approximate is fine for the two chances -- they are unmetered by construction (see src/Core.TypeScript/belief/dual-score.ts) and no decision is keyed to their exact values.
satelliteChain: depth 1. The HUB is the `claim` content address (surface + hypothesis, length-prefixed and digested) -- stable for as long as the hypothesis is a thing anyone could propose. The SATELLITE is the row file itself, keyed by (date partition, body content address), one per witness, never rewritten. The year/month/day folders are the colder-with-depth axis that DV2.0-with-recursive-satellites asks for: a reader who wants this quarter opens one day-range of folders and never touches the rest.
demotionPlan: Age, with the date partition as the mechanism that already exists: a briefing renders the recent partitions hot and leaves older ones on disk, read only when a claim id is looked up directly. Nothing moves out of git, because nothing needs to -- see breaksFirst: the pressure is on what is RENDERED into a context, not on what is stored. A row whose surface has been deleted is retired outright (see liftsWhen), which is a deletion rather than a demotion.
liftsWhen: Per row: when the SURFACE it names no longer exists, the hypothesis cannot be re-proposed against it and the row can be deleted -- a real, checkable exit that most register rows do not have. For the directory as a whole: nothing lifts it, because a factory that stops recording negative results goes back to rediscovering them at full price, which is the cost this ledger exists to stop paying.
reason: Aaron 2026-09-11: "any ledger that's stored in git should not be a single file, it should use partitioning and date based folders like we already described and can also take advantage of our zetaid if needed." This row is that shape's registration: one append-only file per row under db/refutations/YYYY/MM/DD/<zetaid>.json, no file ever rewritten, so the history cost is the rows themselves rather than a fresh copy of the whole ledger per append -- the tick-latest.json failure mode, avoided by construction rather than by promise. The ceiling is 12 against 3 measured rows and is TIGHT ON PURPOSE: the rate above is one day's seed figure, the first crossing is the signal, and re-pinning costs one line plus a re-measured rate.
